s: Under Article 124(2) of the Constitution, the President appoints a Judge of the Supreme Court after consulting the
o: Chief Justice of the concerned High Court
x: Article 124(2) requires consultation with the Chief Justice of India for appointment of a Supreme Court Judge. For appointments of other judges, consultation with the CJI is compulsory.
tq: Identify the constitutional authority specifically associated with the appointment power.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The First Judges Case, generally associated with S.P. Gupta, held that
o: consultation did not mean concurrence and executive primacy prevailed
consultation with the Chief Justice of India meant concurrence
the collegium consisted of the CJI and four senior-most judges
x: The First Judges Case, decided in 1981 and reported in 1982, held that consultation did not mean concurrence and recognised executive primacy in judicial appointments.
tq: Use the case-to-holding distinction to separate the three Judges Cases.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the ruling in the Second Judges Case of 1993?
o: It held that consultation means concurrence and gave primacy to the judiciary.
It struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment.
It upheld executive primacy in judicial appointments.
It expanded the collegium to the CJI and four senior-most judges.
x: The Second Judges Case held that consultation means concurrence, established judicial primacy and gave rise to the collegium consisting initially of the CJI and two senior-most judges.
tq: Match the landmark case with its distinctive constitutional consequence.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The collegium was expanded to the Chief Justice of India and four senior-most Supreme Court judges by the
x: The Third Judges Case, arising from the Presidential Reference under Article 143 in 1998, expanded the Supreme Court collegium to the CJI and four senior-most judges.
tq: Discriminate between closely related judicial decisions by the numerical composition they established.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Judges Cases:
1. The First Judges Case gave primacy to the executive.
2. The Second Judges Case created the collegium system.
3. The Third Judges Case reduced the collegium to the CJI and two senior-most judges.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: the Third Judges Case expanded the collegium to the CJI and four senior-most judges.
tq: Find the altered numerical detail in the statement about the Third Judges Case.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The Fourth Judges Case of 2015 is associated with which of the following outcomes?
o: Creation of the original collegium of three judges
Abolition of judicial primacy in appointments
Striking down of the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act, with restoration of the collegium
Validation of the NJAC Act and the 99th Amendment
x: In SCAORA v. Union of India, decided in 2015, the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act and restored the collegium system.
tq: Use the outcome of the case rather than its title to identify the correct option.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to the collegium system, consider the following statements:
1. It is expressly mentioned in the Constitution of India.
2. It is a judicial creation arising from the Three Judges Cases.
3. It has been in its present form since 1998.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false because the collegium has no express mention in the Constitution or in any constitutional amendment.
tq: Test the distinction between a constitutional provision and a judicially evolved mechanism.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly represents the High Court collegium?
o: The Union Law Minister and two eminent persons
The Chief Justice of India and four senior-most Supreme Court judges
The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court and two senior-most judges of that High Court
The Governor and two senior-most judges of the concerned High Court
x: The High Court collegium consists of the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court and its two senior-most judges. Proposals for High Court appointments are initiated by the High Court Chief Justice.
tq: Separate the composition of the High Court collegium from the Supreme Court collegium.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly states the role of the High Court Chief Justice in the collegium process?
o: The High Court Chief Justice initiates proposals for appointments to the High Court.
The High Court Chief Justice appoints Supreme Court judges.
The High Court Chief Justice selects the two eminent persons in the NJAC.
The High Court Chief Justice ratifies the 99th Amendment.
x: Proposals for appointments to a High Court are initiated by the Chief Justice of that High Court through the High Court collegium.
tq: Ask who performs the initiating function rather than who formally appoints.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: As of June 2026, which one of the following was NOT a member of the Supreme Court collegium?
x: The Supreme Court collegium in June 2026 comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh and P.S. Narasimha. Justice J.K. Maheshwari had retired before that composition was reported.
tq: Use the current-membership list to identify the excluded name.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Justice B.R. Gavai was succeeded as Chief Justice of India by Justice Surya Kant after Justice Gavai's retirement in
x: Justice B.R. Gavai retired in November 2025 and was succeeded by Justice Surya Kant as Chief Justice of India.
tq: Distinguish the closely placed dates in a recent constitutional appointment sequence.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was created through the
x: The NJAC was created by the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014, along with the NJAC Act, 2014.
tq: Match the constitutional body with the specific amendment that created it.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 inserted which provision in the Constitution in connection with the NJAC?
x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 124A, among related provisions, to provide for the National Judicial Appointments Commission.
tq: Test the exact Article number associated with a constitutional amendment.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The NJAC Act, 2014 came into force on
x: The NJAC Act came into force on 13 April 2015. The date 31 December 2014 refers to Presidential assent to the 99th Amendment and the NJAC legislation.
tq: Separate the dates of assent, commencement and judicial invalidation.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the enactment of the NJAC framework:
1. The 99th Constitutional Amendment was passed by the Lok Sabha on 13 August 2014.
2. It was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 14 August 2014.
3. It received Presidential assent on 31 December 2014.
4. It was ratified by 16 States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct: the two Houses passed the measure on 13 and 14 August 2014, 16 States ratified it, and Presidential assent was given on 31 December 2014.
tq: Check each date and numerical detail independently before selecting the coded combination.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following was NOT a component of the six-member NJAC proposed under the 99th Amendment?
o: The two senior-most Supreme Court judges
x: The NJAC comprised the CJI as Chairperson, two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons. The Attorney-General of India was not a member.
tq: Find the wrong authority inserted into a specified constitutional composition.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The proposal relating to representation of a person from the SC, ST, OBC, minority or women categories concerned the selection of
o: the two eminent persons in the NJAC
the two senior-most Supreme Court judges
x: One of the two eminent persons in the proposed NJAC was to be selected from among persons belonging to SC, ST, OBC, minority or women categories.
tq: Link a qualification condition to the correct component of a constitutional body.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The Venkatachaliah Commission, which recommended the establishment of an NJAC, was appointed in 2000 under the Prime Ministership of
x: The Venkatachaliah Commission was appointed in 2000 during the Prime Ministership of Atal Bihari Vajpayee and recommended an NJAC.
tq: Combine the commission's recommendation with its year and political context.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: In SCAORA v. Union of India, the 2015 judgment striking down the NJAC was delivered by a five-judge Bench led by
x: The five-judge Bench in the Fourth Judges Case was led by Justice J.S. Khehar and struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment by a 4:1 majority.
tq: Distinguish the presiding judge from the lone dissenting judge in the same case.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: Who was the lone judge to dissent from the decision striking down the NJAC?
x: Justice J. Chelameswar was the lone dissenter and upheld the NJAC, whereas the majority declared the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act unconstitutional.
tq: Use the majority-dissent distinction as the decisive clue in a case-based question.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Third Judges Case expands the collegium to five members
B. First Judges Case recognises executive primacy
C. Fourth Judges Case strikes down the NJAC
D. Second Judges Case establishes judicial primacy and the collegium
x: The correct sequence is First Judges Case (1981), Second Judges Case (1993), Third Judges Case (1998), and Fourth Judges Case (2015).
tq: Anchor the sequence with the earliest and latest Judges Cases, then place the two intervening cases by year.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about the functioning of the collegium:
1. The Government conducts Intelligence Bureau background checks on recommended candidates.
2. The Government may return a name once for reconsideration.
3. If the collegium reiterates the recommendation, the Government is bound to appoint the person.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. The Government conducts background checks, may return a recommendation once, but is bound to appoint the candidate if the collegium reiterates it.
tq: Test the sequence of scrutiny, one-time reconsideration and binding reiteration.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
A. First Judges Case
B. Second Judges Case
C. Third Judges Case
D. Fourth Judges Case

List-II (Principal development)
1. NJAC and 99th Amendment struck down
2. Executive primacy
3. Collegium expanded to CJI and four senior-most judges
4. Consultation interpreted as concurrence and judicial primacy established

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: The First Judges Case established executive primacy; the Second equated consultation with concurrence; the Third expanded the collegium; and the Fourth struck down the NJAC framework.
tq: Start from the sure pair of the First Judges Case and eliminate incompatible codes.
sec: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment  [APPSC]

s: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 was enacted under which constitutional provision relating to the composition of the Supreme Court?
x: Article 124(1) provides the constitutional basis for determining the number of judges of the Supreme Court. Parliament may increase the number by law, and such an amendment requires only a simple majority.
tq: Match the statutory mechanism with the correct constitutional provision.
sec: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly represents the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice of India, in the years indicated?
x: The strength was 8 in 1950, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986 and 31 from 2009. These figures include the Chief Justice of India.
tq: Use the complete numerical sequence rather than relying on a single familiar figure.
sec: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the strength of the Supreme Court:
1. The 2019 amendment raised the sanctioned strength to 34, including the Chief Justice of India.
2. The 2019 amendment received presidential assent on 10 August 2019.
3. The 2019 amendment replaced the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The 2019 amendment amended the 1956 Act; it did not replace it.
tq: Identify the wrong legislative relationship in the final statement.
sec: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to the 2026 increase in the strength of the Supreme Court, consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 was issued under Article 123.
2. The Ordinance was notified on 16 May 2026.
3. It replaced the figure 'thirty-three' with 'thirty-seven'.
4. A Bill to replace the Ordinance was listed for the Monsoon Session of 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct. The 2026 Ordinance was promulgated under Article 123, notified on 16 May, raised the number from 33 to 37 additional judges apart from the CJI, and was proposed to be replaced by a Bill in the Monsoon Session.
tq: Check each date, constitutional authority and legislative consequence separately.
sec: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following stages relating to the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court in chronological order:
A. Strength fixed at 26
B. Strength fixed at 8
C. Strength fixed at 31
D. Strength fixed at 18
x: The chronological sequence is 1950 (8), 1977 (18), 1986 (26) and 2009 (31).
tq: Anchor the sequence with the earliest and latest strength figures.
sec: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 127 of the Constitution, an ad hoc judge of the Supreme Court may be appointed when
o: the sanctioned strength of the Court is increased
a quorum of permanent judges is lacking
the office of the Chief Justice of India is vacant
a retired judge refuses to sit in the Court
x: Article 127 applies when there is no quorum of permanent judges available to hold or continue a sitting of the Supreme Court.
tq: Associate the exceptional appointment with the specific constitutional trigger.
sec: Retired and ad hoc judges - Articles 127, 128; additional judges  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements about a retired judge sitting in the Supreme Court under Article 128:
1. The Chief Justice of India requires the President's previous consent.
2. The consent of the retired judge is required.
3. Such a judge exercises all the powers of a judge of the Supreme Court.
4. Such a judge is deemed to be a regular judge of the Supreme Court for all purposes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. A retired judge sitting under Article 128 has the powers of a Supreme Court judge but is not deemed to be a regular judge of the Court.
tq: Spot the absolute legal status claim in the last statement.
sec: Retired and ad hoc judges - Articles 127, 128; additional judges  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding additional judges is correct?
o: Additional judges are appointed under Article 128 for temporary vacancies in the Supreme Court.
Additional judges exist in High Courts under Article 224, but there are no additional judges in the Supreme Court.
Additional judges may be appointed in the Supreme Court under Article 224.
Additional judges are appointed only in the Supreme Court when its workload increases.
x: Article 224 deals with additional and acting judges of High Courts. The Supreme Court has no provision for additional judges of this kind.
tq: Distinguish the similar-sounding categories attached to the Supreme Court and High Courts.
sec: Retired and ad hoc judges - Articles 127, 128; additional judges  [APPSC]

s:
Article 131 confers exclusive original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in which of the following disputes?
1. Between the Government of India and one or more States
2. Between the Government of India and some States on one side and other States on the other
3. Between two or more States
4. Between two private companies incorporated in different States
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 describe the federal disputes covered by Article 131. A dispute between private companies does not fall within this exclusive original jurisdiction.
tq: Separate federal-unit disputes from ordinary private litigation.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is NOT excluded from the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131?
o: An inter-State river-water dispute governed by Article 262
A dispute between the Government of India and one or more States concerning their legal rights
A dispute under a pre-Constitution treaty or agreement
A matter concerning the Finance Commission under Article 280
x: A dispute between the Union and one or more States concerning legal rights is within Article 131. Pre-Constitution agreements, inter-State river-water disputes and Finance Commission matters are excluded.
tq: Find the one included category among constitutionally excluded matters.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Original jurisdiction over federal disputes — Article 131
Review of Supreme Court judgments — Article 143
x: Article 131 deals with the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction over federal disputes. Article 143 concerns advisory jurisdiction, Article 137 review, and Article 136 Special Leave to Appeal.
tq: Use the article-number distinction among closely related Supreme Court jurisdictions.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 is original in nature.
2. Article 32 jurisdiction is exclusive to the Supreme Court because High Courts cannot issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
3. The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Article 131 is exclusive in respect of the specified federal disputes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original writ jurisdiction, but it is not exclusive because High Courts may issue writs under Article 226.
tq: Discriminate between original jurisdiction that is exclusive and original jurisdiction shared with High Courts.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s: The jurisdiction to decide disputes relating to the election of the President and Vice-President of India is
o: appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136
original jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226
original, exclusive and final jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 71
advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143
x: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with original, exclusive and final jurisdiction over disputes concerning the election of the President and Vice-President.
tq: Link the special election jurisdiction with its distinctive constitutional features.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following matters falls outside the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?
1. An election dispute concerning the Parliament
2. An election dispute concerning a State Legislature
3. A dispute between two or more States
4. A dispute between the Union and one or more States
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Election disputes concerning Parliament and State Legislatures are outside the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and ordinarily go to the High Courts. Union-State and inter-State federal disputes are covered by Article 131.
tq: Separate legislative election disputes from Article 131 federal disputes.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s: The curative petition jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is associated with which of the following cases?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
S. R. Bommai v. Union of India
x: The Supreme Court evolved the curative petition in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), permitting a limited remedy after dismissal of a review petition in exceptional circumstances.
tq: Associate the procedural innovation with the case that created it.
sec: Original jurisdiction - Article 131  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the constitutional safeguard relating to the removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court?
o: Removal by the President after an address by Parliament passed by a special majority
Removal by the Chief Justice of India after a parliamentary inquiry
Removal by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers
Removal by Parliament through a simple majority
x: A Supreme Court Judge can be removed by the President only after both Houses of Parliament pass an address supported by the prescribed special majority.
tq: Identify the authority and the required majority instead of accepting a simple-majority trap.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the salaries of Judges of the Supreme Court:
1. Their salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. Their salaries may be varied to their disadvantage during a Financial Emergency.
3. Parliament fixes their salaries by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because salaries cannot be varied to a judge’s disadvantage except as permitted during a Financial Emergency; the safeguard is that ordinary executive action cannot reduce them.
tq: Split the statements by distinguishing the general salary safeguard from the Financial Emergency exception.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s: The conduct of a Judge of the Supreme Court may be discussed in Parliament only during:
o: A motion for the removal of the Judge
A discussion initiated by the Law Minister
A debate on the annual budget
x: Under Article 121, the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge cannot be discussed in Parliament except upon a motion for the Judge’s removal.
tq: Use the constitutional exception rather than the broad prohibition alone.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 129 — Supreme Court as a Court of Record and power to punish contempt
Article 121 — Appointment of Supreme Court Judges
Article 146 — Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
x: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a Court of Record and gives it the power to punish contempt of itself. The other Articles are associated with parliamentary discussion of judicial conduct, court staff and salaries respectively.
tq: Match the Article with its precise subject and reject neighbouring constitutional provisions.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s:
With reference to post-retirement practice by judges, consider the following statements:
1. A retired Supreme Court Judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India.
2. A retired High Court Judge may plead only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts.
3. These restrictions are intended to protect judicial independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court Judge from practice in India, while Article 220 permits a retired High Court Judge to practise only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts.
tq: Compare the different post-retirement restrictions applicable to Supreme Court and High Court Judges.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Supreme Court — Article 129
2. High Court — Article 215
3. Supreme Court salaries — Consolidated Fund of India
4. High Court salaries — Consolidated Fund of India
x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. High Court salaries are charged on the State fund, whereas the pension of High Court Judges is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India; therefore pair 4 is false.
tq: Separate the fund charged with High Court salaries from the fund charged with High Court pensions.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s: The convention that the senior-most Judge should ordinarily be appointed as the Chief Justice of India was broken in:
x: The convention was broken in 1973 in the appointment of A.N. Ray and again in 1977 in the appointment of M.H. Beg. The Second Judges Case subsequently affirmed the senior-most Judge convention.
tq: Use the paired-year clue and distinguish the convention from the later judicial position.
sec: Independence safeguards - statement-based

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Abolition of appeals to the Privy Council
B. Establishment of the Federal Court
C. Inauguration of the Supreme Court
D. Shift of the Supreme Court to Tilak Marg
x: The Federal Court was established in 1937, Privy Council appeals were abolished in 1949, the Supreme Court was inaugurated in 1950, and it shifted to Tilak Marg in 1958.
tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two transitional constitutional events.
sec: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

s: Who was the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court of India?
x: Justice M. Fathima Beevi became the first woman Judge of the Supreme Court of India in 1989.
tq: Discriminate among women judges by identifying the first appointment and its year.
sec: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court of India:
1. Its constitutional basis is contained in Articles 124 to 147.
2. It forms Part V, Chapter IV of the Constitution.
3. It is the final interpreter of the Constitution and the guardian of Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. The Supreme Court is dealt with in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147, and performs the role of final constitutional interpreter and guardian of Fundamental Rights.
tq: Check whether the constitutional location and functional description are stated together correctly.
sec: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

s: Under Article 130, the Supreme Court may sit at a place other than Delhi when:
o: The Union Cabinet directs it to do so
Parliament passes a resolution by a simple majority
The President orders it on the advice of the Governor concerned
The Chief Justice of India appoints the place with the approval of the President
x: Article 130 permits the Supreme Court to sit in Delhi or at such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may appoint with the approval of the President.
tq: Ask who would perform the institutional function and who gives the required approval.
sec: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

s: Which one of the following statements about the seating arrangements of the Supreme Court is correct?
o: Every case must be heard by a bench of at least five Judges
The Constitution prescribes that all appeals must be heard by seven Judges
Constitutional matters are heard only by a single Judge
Usual benches consist of two or three Judges, while constitutional matters require at least five Judges
x: The usual benches of the Supreme Court comprise two or three Judges. A bench of at least five Judges is required for questions involving interpretation of the Constitution.
tq: Separate the ordinary bench size from the constitutional-bench minimum.
sec: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

s: Which of the following sets correctly represents the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under the Constitution?
o: Articles 132, 133 and 134 — constitutional, civil and criminal appeals respectively
Articles 129, 130 and 131 — constitutional, civil and criminal appeals respectively
Articles 136, 137 and 138 — civil, criminal and advisory appeals respectively
Articles 141, 142 and 143 — constitutional, civil and criminal appeals respectively
x: Article 132 deals with constitutional appeals, Article 133 with civil appeals and Article 134 with criminal appeals from High Courts.
tq: Start from the sure Article–jurisdiction pair and eliminate the nearby jurisdiction provisions.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s: Special Leave Petition under Article 136 is best described as:
o: A discretionary appeal from any court or tribunal, except military tribunals
A compulsory appeal available only in civil cases
A review petition against the Supreme Court’s own judgment
An automatic appeal available against every administrative order
x: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from judgments or orders of any court or tribunal in India, except those relating to the armed forces.
tq: Watch the words discretionary, any court or tribunal and the military exception.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments.
2. Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India.
3. Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to make orders for completing the legislative process.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 142 empowers the Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, not to complete the legislative process as such.
tq: Reject the wrong-purpose trap by distinguishing complete justice from legislative power.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: Article 142 authorises the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice. Article 129 concerns the Court of Record, Article 143 advisory jurisdiction and Article 145 rules of the Court.
tq: Match the Article with its exact power rather than with a neighbouring Supreme Court jurisdiction.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s:
With reference to Article 142, consider the following statements:
1. It enables the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice.
2. High Courts possess an identical constitutional power under the same Article.
3. The Supreme Court has used this power in matters concerning Tamil Nadu Bills and the Right to Safe Travel.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. High Courts do not possess an equivalent power under Article 142; the power belongs specifically to the Supreme Court.
tq: Use the constitutional-level comparison to identify the false claim of an equivalent High Court power.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s: The minimum number of Judges required for hearing a constitutional question before the Supreme Court is:
x: Article 145 requires at least five Judges for hearing a case involving a substantial question of interpretation of the Constitution.
tq: Distinguish the constitutional-bench minimum from the usual two- or three-Judge bench.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s: The Supreme Court is a Court of Record under Article 129. Which one of the following follows from this status?
o: Its advisory opinions automatically amend the Constitution
It may punish for contempt of itself
It may remove any High Court Judge without parliamentary procedure
Its records can never be reviewed by the Court
x: Article 129 recognises the Supreme Court as a Court of Record and expressly gives it the power to punish contempt of itself. Court of Record status does not confer the other powers listed.
tq: Apply the legal consequence directly associated with the term Court of Record.
sec: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

s: Which of the following statements about the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 is correct?
o: It defines only civil contempt and leaves criminal contempt undefined
It defines civil and criminal contempt, while the Constitution itself does not define contempt
It abolishes the Supreme Court’s constitutional contempt power
It applies only to proceedings before High Courts
x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil and criminal contempt. The Constitution confers contempt powers on the Supreme Court and High Courts but does not itself define contempt.
tq: Separate the statutory definition from the constitutional conferment of contempt power.
